warmup_extension_Q3_example.action: locate an erroneous rectangle cell or middle-term sum
warmup_extension_Q3_example.original_task: A rectangle model gives x^2 + 6x + 6 for (x+3)(x+2). Without multiplying the entire expression again, identify the cell calculation or grouping that must change.
warmup_extension_Q3_example.solution: x^2+5x+6; the two linear cells contribute 3x and 2x, so the middle coefficient is 5.

warmup_extension_Q3_alternative.action: predict effect of a one-unit factor change
warmup_extension_Q3_alternative.original_task: The rectangle for (x+3)(x+2) is extended by one unit on the second side. How does the product change?
warmup_extension_Q3_alternative.solution: It increases by x+3, because the added strip is (x+3) by 1.

smarty_pants_current_lesson_example.title: Add One Strip: Tile Display Design
smarty_pants_current_lesson_example.new_authored_scenario: A school club represents a rectangular mosaic with side lengths x^2+2x+3 and x+4 unit tiles. It can make the design one tile-row taller while keeping its width unchanged.
connected_questions: Draw a 2-by-3 generic rectangle and write an expanded expression for the original tile count.
Predict how many tiles the extra row needs without expanding a second full product.
Write the new tile-count expression and verify the difference algebraically.
For x=2, find both counts and explain why the change equals the width.
smarty_pants_current_lesson_example.teacher_note: This is a structure test, not an approved final student prompt. Confirm polynomial length units and visual model are appropriate to taught lesson.
